title: Trump gets MAGA backlash over ‘amnesty’ comments | CNN Politics
text:
Source: CNN

It remains unlikely that President Donald Trump would ever sign off on giving millions of undocumented immigrants a path to legal status.

But after a brutal 2026 election for Republicans, he’s talking about it again. And it’s setting off a major — and seemingly unnecessary — backlash in his base at about the worst possible time for the GOP.

Consider it just the latest in a series of bizarre political moves from Trump both before and after last week’s bruising midterms.

The internal discord kicked off Sunday night, whenCBS News’ “60 Minutes”aired an interview in which Trump acknowledged his deportations had been “too tough” and cost Republicans in the election.

But then the president went a step further, suggesting he’d be open to legalizing the status of millions of undocumented migrants.

Trump summarized the idea as: “Get the killers out, get the rapists out, get all the rough ones out, get the drug dealers out. But let the people that are here — and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years — work a deal for them.”

Trump sometimes floats such things and then quickly backs off them. But by Monday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin signaledthis wasn’t just Trump freelancing.

Mullin assured there would be “no amnesty” and that the administration’s law enforcement approach “isn’t going to change.” But he said that Trump had signaled a desire to work with Democrats.

“Now, if we want to have an immigration reform to where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this, that’ll be up to Congress,” Mullin said, referring to the Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, which allowed undocumented migrants who arrived as children to stay. (It’s likely, given the context, he meant to say “legal permanent residents.”)

Trump added at an impromptu press conference late Monday afternoon: “There’s no amnesty. … There won’t be amnesty. Somebody suggested, will there be amnesty? No.”

But while Mullin and Trump can deny this is “amnesty” all day long, that’s not how it’s playing — or going to play — with Trump’s base.

The flap has set off an extraordinary backlash — with many Trump allies like theHeritage Foundationand theHouse Freedom Caucusposting on X, “No amnesty,” without specifically pointing to Trump’s comments.

Florida GOP Gov. Ron DeSantis — who has recently stepped forward to criticize a number of the Trump administration’s moves and political strategies —pointed to his own past commentssignaling there should be no exceptions to deportations.

Missouri GOP Rep. Bob Onder was more direct, posting, “NO amnesty for illegal aliens” in response to the “60 Minutes” interview.

When the official White House rapid response account on X claimed that Trump wasn’t talking about amnesty, a reporter at the Federalistcalled it “insulting.”

And others signaled it was just the latest thumb in the eye of the president’s base.

Former Trump adviser Steve Cortes said, “If President Trump struck an amnesty deal with the Democrat-controlled Congress, it would bea bigger betrayal than starting the foolish war in Iran.” GOP strategist Ryan Girdusky said Trump was “proposing an idea that will kill the party.”

“And now amnesty. Seriously?” podcast host Megyn Kelly said.

It is indeed politically perplexing.

Trump could just as easily have signaled a bit of a retreat on mass deportations without going into pathways to legal status. His base wouldn’t have loved it, but it might have understood it. And such a limited retreat would have at least been targeted at the real, big political problem for his party.

But Trump’s comments are even more confusing because it’s very unlikely this idea will ever lead anywhere.

This isn’t the first time he has floated some sort of pathway to citizenship, with each episode prompting a similar backlash from his base.

Bothbeforeand after he won the 2016 election, he leaned ona path to legal status for Dreamers: “We’re going to work something out that’s going to make people happy and proud.”

In January 2018, he said he wouldaccept a lengthy path to citizenship for DACA-eligible immigrantsbecause it was “going to happen at some point in the future.”

He signaled an openness on working with Democrats on Dreamers againafter his 2024 election. And in June 2025, he floated “some kind of a temporary pass” for migrant workers, apparently because business interests expressed concern about how his deportations impacted industry needs.

The thing is, if Trump wanted to pursue some kind of deal that would legalize these people’s status, he could possibly make it happen. I wrotenearly a decade agoabout how Trump’s control over his base could make him the one modern president to get this done. And that remains true.

But it’s in all likelihood not going to happen. In order to push it through, Trump would undoubtedly have to alienate huge chunks of his base which, as noted,already isn’t thrilled with him. It would be self-defeating. Any political gain would come at the expense of the total fracturing of MAGA.

Which means that, a week out from massive GOP losses, Trump is provoking his base over something that in all likelihood isn’t going to happen and that he didn’t need to float.

But this is also a president who seems to do and say what he wants these days, with little concern for how it plays politically and what problems it might create for his party.

Maybe this becomes a really a major initiative of Trump’s. But don’t be surprised if he tucks his tail and runs from it pretty quickly.
